name: Armyworm caterpillar feeding complex
summary: A late-season caterpillar feeding differential for hemp. Armyworm larvae can defoliate foliage and enter buds or flowers, but species-level identification requires larval morphology rather than damage pattern alone.
indicators: Caterpillar larvae are present with fresh irregular chewing injury
Severe feeding skeletonizes or strips leaves toward the midribs
Larvae entering buds or flowers leave feeding injury together with silk and frass
Larval head/body markings support fall armyworm, true armyworm, or another armyworm identification
exclusions: No larvae or fresh frass are found and damage is old
Characteristic looping larvae support cabbage looper
Adult Japanese beetles are actively skeletonizing tissue

progression.description: Larvae chew irregular holes and remove expanding leaf area.
High feeding pressure can skeletonize leaves or strip tissue to major veins.
Later larvae can enter reproductive tissue, leaving silk, frass, and damaged floral material.

confirmation: Collect or clearly photograph representative larvae and use morphology for species-level assignment.
Treat frass plus an active larva as stronger evidence than holes alone.
immediateActions: Inspect fresh feeding fronts, buds, and flowers for larvae and frass.
Record larval size and density because damage potential changes with instar and population.
correctivePlan: Use an IPM response based on confirmed caterpillar identity, population, crop stage, and locally legal hemp options.
prevention: Scout late-season foliage and reproductive tissue for egg masses and young larvae.
Use monitoring and beneficial-conservation practices where appropriate.
warnings: Armyworm damage overlaps other caterpillar feeding.
Do not identify species from leaf holes or frass alone.

sources.title: Insect Pests of Industrial Hemp in Missouri
supportedClaims: Spotted cucumber beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and floral tissue, producing holes and ragged edges, while larvae can feed on root hairs and root tips.
Tarnished plant bug feeding on young hemp leaves, stems, buds, and flowers can produce chlorotic spots, leaf curling, terminal stunting, distorted buds, and bud abortion.
Dectes texanus larvae can bore inside hemp stems and pith, producing internal galleries, wilting, dieback, swollen or split stems, and increased breakage risk.
Cabbage looper larvae feed on hemp leaves, often from lower-leaf undersides upward, producing large irregular holes and potentially damaging floral buds.
Japanese beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and can skeletonize leaves between veins; adults are metallic green with bronze wing covers and often aggregate.
Armyworm larvae can create irregular holes and skeletonization and may enter hemp buds or flowers, where silk and frass can accompany feeding injury.
Hemp insect pressure varies by region, growth stage, and variety, so damage morphology without organism evidence should not be treated as species confirmation.
